items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the insurance law, in relation to electronic delivery of insurance notices and posting insurance policies on the internet
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S5249

TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the insurance law, in relation to electronic delivery of
insurance notices and posting insurance policies on the internet

PURPOSE:

To permit insurance notices and documents to be delivered electronically
with policyholder consent. To allow state-approved insurance policies to
be  accessed on the internet instead of being mailed unless specifically
requested by the policyholder

SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 adds new section 3114  to  the  Insurance  Law.  Section  3114
permits  insurers  to  deliver insurance notices and documents electron-
ically with the policyholder consent.

Section 2 adds new section 3455  to  the  Insurance  Law.  Section  3455
permits a property-casualty insurance company to elect to post state-ap-
proved  insurance  policies  and  endorsements  on the company's website
Policyholders would be able to request a free paper copy of  the  insur-
ance policy.

Section 3 is the effective date.

JUSTIFICATION:

Section 1: There has been an increasing trend in today's technologically
advanced  society toward communicating electronically.  Insurance compa-
nies would like to provide the option to their  customers  of  receiving
notices and documents electronically.

Currently, the Department of Financial Services has advised that the use
of  electronic communications in insurance related transaction is gener-
ally permitted, as long consumers have consented to doing business elec-
tronically. However, there is a significant exception to this allowance.
Electronic delivery of notices is not allowed if a statute or regulation
specifically provides for a document or notice to be "mailed." There are
several statutes  and  regulations  that  still  reference  delivery  by
"mail".

This bill would allow all insurance notices and document to be delivered
electronically as long as the consumer affirmatively consents to receiv-
ing such notices and documents electronically. The bill includes several
safeguards  designed  to  protect the consumer.  This includes requiring
insurers to provide consumers with a clear notice of their rights before
consent is given. Consumers would have the right to withdraw consent  at
any  time  Before  giving consent the consumer must be provided with the
hardware and software requirements to receive documents  electronically.

Also,  the  consumer must consent electronically in a manner that demon-
strates that they can access the information in the electronic form that
will be used for electronic document delivery. In the event the  insurer
makes  hardware  of  software change, they must notify the consumer. Any
time an insurer has reason to believe the  electronic  transmission  has
failed  to  reach the consumer, they must deliver the notice or document
by another delivery method.

Section 2: Each year property and casualty insurance companies print and
then mail millions of  policy  contract  booklets  to  their  customers.
Often, these policies can exceed fifty pages in length.  Surveys suggest
consumer's  often toss their policies into the recycle bins without ever
reading them. While e-commerce laws have helped to eliminate some of the
waste, the process still has serious limitations.

This legislation would allow the posting of standard approved  insurance
policies  and  endorsements on the insurance company's website, provided
that the policy remains accessible for as  long  as  the  policy  is  in
force.  Expired policies and endorsements would be required to be avail-
able for five years, and upon request after that.

The policies and endorsements must be posted in a  manner  that  enables
the  policyholder  to  print  and save the policy and endorsements using
programs or applications widely available on the internet  and  free  to
use.  The insurance company is required to provide with each declaration
page a description of the exact policy and endorsement  forms  purchased
by  the  insured,  a  description of the policyholder's right to receive
upon request and without charge, a paper copy of the policy and endorse-
ments by mail and the internet address where their policy  and  endorse-
ments are posted.

Personal  identifying  information would not be posted. This legislation
applies to insurance policy and endorsements as approved by the  Depart-
ment of Financial Services.

The benefits to the insurance consumer are many. First, for the prospec-
tive  insurance  buyer,  he or she can look at the approved policies and
better compare the provisions of competitors. Second,  this  legislation
is  environmentally  friendly; it reduces unnecessary and unwanted mail-
ings. Third, there are no privacy concerns,  as  policy  contracts  arid
endorsements do not contain any personal identifying information Fourth,
electronic  policy  contracts  create  additional  features that are not
possible with paper contracts, for example, companies could augment  the
policies  with FAQs, annotations, chat functionality for answering ques-
tions and other content to help consumers better understand their  poli-
cies.  Enabling  laws  have  been  approved  in  at least thirteen other
states.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

This  act  shall  take  effect  on the ninetieth day after it shall have
become law.

items.memoText:
VETO MESSAGE - No. 274

TO THE SENATE:

I am returning herewith, without my approval, the following bill:

Senate Bill Number 5249-B, entitled:

    "AN ACT to amend the insurance law, in relation to electronic deliv-
      ery   of   property/casualty   insurance   notices   and   posting
      property/casualty insurance policies on the internet"

    NOT APPROVED

  This bill would amend the Insurance Law  to  allow  insurers  to  send
property/casualty  notices  or  documents  to  their customers electron-
ically, provided the customer gives consent.

  I fully support the intent of this bill,  which  allows  consumers  to
choose  whether to receive property/casualty notices and documents elec-
tronically. As drafted, however, this bill raises  substantial  consumer
protection  concerns. First, the bill's opt-out provisions are in direct
contrast to the prior consent requirements  of  the  State's  Electronic
Signatures and Records Act ("ESRA"). Under ESRA, a consumer must provide
consent  for the electronic transmission of documents before any notifi-
cations are sent. Here, the consumer can only "opt-out" after the  elec-
tronic  transmission  has been sent, which directly contradicts the ESRA
consent requirement.

  Second, the bill does not require insurers to  conspicuously  flag  or
otherwise  alert  the  consumer  that an attached document may contain a
cancellation notice, notice of non-renewal, or other important  informa-
tion.  Despite  containing  critical  information, the text of the email
could therefore be as vague as "Important  Notice"  or  even  simply  "A
notice  to  you  has  been  posted on the website." Given the barrage of
electronic notices that consumers receive each day, it is highly  proba-
ble  that  such  an important notification will be overlooked.  Specific
warnings in subject lines of emails are  therefore  essential  to  alert
consumers that the email contains a cancellation notice, renewal notice,
or the like.

  For these reasons, I am therefore constrained to veto this bill.

  The bill is disapproved.                    (signed) ANDREW M. CUOMO

                               __________
